name: Cement
lede: Cement is a muted grey with a trace of green, the color of dried mortar; the books say more about the blue once sold for coloring cement than about the grey.

sections.title: A grey with a few sources
sections.body: Cement is filed in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 (block 265), in Maerz and Paul (1930), where it is first recorded in 1922, and in Ridgway (1912), whose near twin is called Light Olive-Grey [1]. None of the books we hold defines the grey itself. They use the word *cement* for the building material [2][3].

sections.title: Cement blue
sections.body:
The color connection in the books runs the other way: a blue was named after the material. The Pigment Compendium records *cement blue* as a name for manganese blue, a barium manganate sold as a pigment because it colored Portland cement [4]. Ball says it was patented in 1935 by the German color cartel IG Farben and first used to color cement [2]. Coles says it was discovered in 1907, reached commercial production in the mid-1930s, and was dropped in the 1990s [3]. The Compendium gives its production as lasting to the early 1990s [4].

Lime, the base of cement, is made by heating limestone to about 900 degrees C, and slaked lime hardens as it takes up carbon dioxide [4]. A soft white mineral first described in 1934 is named for its occurrence in Portland cement [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, this color covers at least five per cent of the canvas, within six units of color distance, in 2,812 paintings, or 12 per cent [5]. It is nearly always a light color: 80 per cent of its appearances are in the highlights [5]. It is a photograph-of-varnish match, not a pigment test [5].

Impressionism carries it in 38 of 140 works, more than twice the archive rate [5]. Eugène Boudin has it in 22 of 33 paintings, about five and a half times the rate [5]. The strongest single match is Ikkyū Sōjun's ink painting *Listening to the Wind in the Pines*, of about 1400, where it fills 86 per cent of the work [5]. Its company is [[ash]], [[sage]] and [[taupe]], the greys that lean green or brown [5].
